name: Kansas
$scopeNote: STATE income tax only. Kansas has no local wage-income tax anywhere -- Kansas's local 'intangibles tax' (Form 200, filed with the county clerk) applies only to INTEREST AND DIVIDEND income, not wages, and is a RETURN-level filing, not employer-withheld -- context-only, same disclosed-scope convention as Iowa's school district surtax and Connecticut's out-of-state credit. Kansas has no FORMAL bilateral reciprocity agreement with any state (no 'resident of state X owes $0 KS tax' exemption the way Michigan/Ohio/Indiana/Kentucky/New Jersey/Iowa's own reciprocity blocks work) -- but KW-100 DOES describe a real, different, WITHHOLDING-LEVEL mechanism for the opposite direction (a KANSAS resident working OUTSIDE Kansas): withhold the Kansas tax otherwise due, LESS whatever the other state withheld, floored at $0. NOW MODELLED: residentWorkingElsewhereCreditLine() in src/taxes/state.ts computes this generically off input.residenceState -- the first state in this project to need a SECOND state's tax computed as a residence-state credit within one calculatePaycheck() call, gated by this file's own residentWorkingElsewhereCredit flag so no other state's behavior changes. No employee-paid unemployment, disability, or paid-leave program exists in Kansas.
$methodComment: KW-100 (Rev. 10-24, 'for wages paid on and after 2024-07-01', still the current guide with no newer revision found -- Kansas's SB 1 (2024) tax reform reduced the state to a genuine 2-bracket system, 5.20%/5.58%). Subtract a per-period allowance, computed CONTINUOUSLY as the annual exemption amount divided by periodsPerYear (per KW-100's own literal instruction), from per-period gross wages, then look up the result in one of Kansas's own two per-period bracket tables (Single, which also covers Head of Household, or Joint) -- all 8 pay periods (Tables 1-8) are published independently and transcribed verbatim, the same convention as New Jersey/Vermont/Connecticut for genuine marginal-bracket states. See kansasExemptionAmount()'s own doc comment in src/taxes/state.ts for why Form K-4's allowance lines are NOT a flat per-allowance multiplier -- each line (personal, spouse, head-of-household, dependent) is worth a different dollar amount.
exemptPretaxComment: KW-100 states directly: 'Kansas law requires withholding on wages. If your cafeteria, 401K, profit sharing, or other employee plan is considered to be wages by the federal government and federal income tax withholding is required, Kansas withholding is also required.' Confirms Kansas tracks the FEDERAL wages-or-not determination exactly (conforms), the same pattern as Michigan/Ohio/Idaho/Connecticut/Iowa/Vermont in this project and the opposite of Pennsylvania's non-conformity.

sources.title: Kansas Department of Revenue -- KW-100 Withholding Tax Guide (Rev. 10-24), Internet Archive copy of ksrevenue.gov captured 2025-03-05
sources.quote: NEW WITHHOLDING TAX RATES for wages paid on or after July 1, 2024 ... EXAMPLE: Esmeralda Espinoza is paid $2,000 semi-monthly. She is married and has one dependent ... $797 x 5.2% = $41.44 ... may be rounded to $41

sources.title: U.S. Department of Labor, ETA -- Significant Provisions of State Unemployment Insurance Laws, Effective January 2025

reciprocity.note: This mechanism is for the OTHER direction (a nonresident of Kansas working here owing $0 KS tax) and Kansas has none -- reciprocalStates deliberately empty, not omitted. This is NOT the same claim as this file's own residentWorkingElsewhereCredit block below, which covers the opposite direction (a Kansas RESIDENT working elsewhere) and is a real, different, KW-100-documented mechanism -- now engine-modelled, see that block.

residentWorkingElsewhereCredit.$comment: KW-100, quoted directly: 'When you employ or pay a Kansas resident for services performed outside Kansas (either full time or part time), withhold from that employee's total wages the amount of withholding tax due Kansas, less the amount of withholding tax required by the other state(s).' Worked example in the source: Jane lives in Kansas, works in Missouri; KS withholding due on her total wages is $250, Missouri withholding is $130 -- $120 (the difference) is withheld for Kansas. 'If the other state's withholding is more than the Kansas amount, then no Kansas withholding tax is due.' ENGINE-CONSUMED as of this pass: presence of this block (any truthy value) is the opt-in gate residentWorkingElsewhereCreditLine() checks on the RESIDENCE state's own ruleset -- when input.residenceState.code is 'KS' and differs from input.workState.code, it computes Kansas's own bracketPerPeriodKansas() tax on the same wages (using input.residenceState.certificate as the K-4 fields -- allowanceRate/personalAllowances/headOfHousehold/dependents, the SAME field names bracketPerPeriodKansas() reads off a normal workState certificate), and emits a KS_SIT_CREDIT line for the shortfall, floored at $0. Verified against KW-100's own Jane/Missouri-shaped example in tests/engine.test.ts (using a synthetic MI work-state figure since this engine doesn't have a Missouri ruleset to test against directly).

knownGaps: Descriptive notes carried from the 2026 file (reciprocity, local-tax rules, method comments) were checked against the 2025 source for the fields this engine computes from; narrative text that only describes 2026 history should be read as background.

suiEmployer.$comment: Normalized employer-side unemployment parameters — the shape src/taxes/state.ts reads. The detailed unemploymentInsurance block above stays the record of research; this exists because that block's shape varies too much between states to compute from directly (wage bases as objects, industry-keyed rate maps, differently-named keys).
suiEmployer.wageBaseSource: DOL Significant Provisions, January 2025 (Wages Subject to Tax)
suiEmployer.newEmployerRateSource: DOL Significant Provisions, January 2025 (New Employer Rate, base rate)
suiEmployer.industryNewEmployerRatesSource: WIRED 2026-09-05, closing this file's own previously-disclosed gap: the same KLRD briefing above states 'New employers within the construction industry are instead charged a contribution rate of 5.55 percent.' src/taxes/state.ts now checks input.employer.suiIndustry['KS'] === 'construction' before falling back to the flat 1.75% newEmployerRate above — chosen over flipping this state to employerSuppliedRateRequired specifically so the many non-construction KS callers keep getting the correct 1.75% by default rather than silently losing their SUI line. A caller who doesn't say what industry they're in gets the general 1.75% rate, the same 'unknown fact, use the general rule' default this engine already applies to an unsupplied stateUnemploymentRate — never inferred from anything else in the paycheck.

supplementalWages: KW-100's own rule, quoted verbatim in this file's sources[] entry above, is genuinely simpler to wire than most states': it doesn't describe an independent Kansas-specific election at all, just an instruction to MIRROR whichever method was used for FEDERAL withholding on the same payment. This engine already has only ONE federal method for a supplemental-categorized earning -- federalSupplementalTax() in src/taxes/federal.ts ALWAYS carves supplemental cash out and taxes it at the flat 22%/37% rate, with no aggregate-federal alternative modelled -- so the federal side of the mirror is always already the flat-rate case, and Kansas following it is unconditional (no employer election field, unlike California/Maryland/Alabama). appliesWhen is still "paid_separately", not "always": KW-100's own alternate branch (adding regular and supplemental together) is exactly what already happens by default when they ARE combined on one cheque, and the generic flatRateSupplementalFromConfig() mechanism already handles that split -- no bespoke function needed for this state, unlike CA/MD.
supplementalWages.source: KW-100, Kansas Withholding Tax Guide (Rev. 10-24), SUPPLEMENTAL WAGES section.

$yearNote: 2025 ruleset: KW-100 (Rev. 10-24), 'new withholding tax rates for wages paid on or after July 1, 2024', was the table in force for all of 2025: 5.2% and 5.58%, $9,160 per personal exemption ($18,320 married filing jointly), $2,320 per dependent and head-of-household allowance. These are the same tables the 2026 file uses; only the unemployment figures differ.
